subject: rla
title: Main Idea, Supporting Details, and Summarizing
objectives: Students will distinguish between the topic of a text and its main idea, and state a main idea as a complete sentence.
Students will locate stated main ideas in paragraphs and whole passages, and determine implied main ideas from the supporting details.
Students will identify the supporting details that develop a main idea and decide which details best support a given claim.
Students will write accurate, objective summaries of informational texts and choose the best summary from a set of options.
Students will recognize the common GED answer traps on main idea questions: too narrow, too broad, not stated, and distorted.
teach:
Lesson overview

Week 1 introduces the reading skill that sits underneath almost every question on the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts (RLA) test: figuring out what a text is mostly about, which details hold that idea up, and how to restate the whole text briefly and accurately. The same skill drives many Social Studies and Science questions and the extended response, so tell learners that early.

Objectives

  • Tell topic from main idea; state a main idea as a sentence.
  • Find stated and implied main ideas.
  • Choose the detail that best supports a claim.
  • Write and choose objective summaries.
  • Spot the four answer traps.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen) and this week's Notes sheet
  • Whiteboard or shared screen; highlighters or markers in two colors
  • Copies of the warm-up paragraph, the three worked-example paragraphs, and the guided-practice passage (all included below)
  • Index cards or a shared document for the exit ticket
  • Week 1 practice items (the tree passage, items 1–6, are used for independent practice)

60-minute timing plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5“Headline it”: learners write an 8-word headline for a paragraph
Direct instruction20Topic vs. main idea; where main ideas live; supporting details and the umbrella test; implied main ideas; summarizing; answer traps; three worked examples
Guided practice15Whole-group apprenticeship passage, five questions
Independent practice15Practice items 1–6 (tree passage); circulate and coach
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; exit ticket; assign the week's study plan

Warm-up (5 minutes): Headline it

Display or read this paragraph aloud. Each learner writes a headline of eight words or fewer that tells a reader what the paragraph is mostly about.

When the Riverside bus route was cut last spring, ridership on the remaining routes did not rise as the transit agency had expected. Instead, many former riders bought used cars, carpooled with coworkers, or stopped making some trips altogether. A survey found that one in five former riders had turned down a job or a class because they could no longer get there. The agency now plans to restore part of the route.

Answers (accept similar): “Bus route cut left many riders stranded” or “Cutting Riverside route hurt riders; agency backtracks.” Contrast two weak headlines: “Riverside bus route” names only the topic; “One in five turned down jobs” names only one detail. A strong headline, like a main idea, says what happened and why it matters.

Direct instruction (20 minutes)

Talking point 1: Topic vs. main idea (3 minutes)

Say: “The topic is the subject, usually a word or short phrase. The main idea is the point the author makes about that topic, and it is always a complete sentence.” Write on the board: Topic: the Riverside bus cut. Main idea: Cutting the Riverside route made life harder for former riders, so the agency is restoring part of it. Ask: “Which of these could be true or false?” Expected: only the main idea, because only a sentence makes a claim. Learners can use this test on their own answers.

Talking point 2: Where main ideas live (3 minutes)

  • First sentence: most common, not guaranteed.
  • After a hook or transition such as a story, question, or link to the last paragraph.
  • Last sentence: details first, then the point.
  • Nowhere: the main idea is implied.

For a whole passage, check the title, the end of paragraph 1, and the conclusion.

Talking point 3: Supporting details and the umbrella test (4 minutes)

Supporting details are the facts, statistics, examples, reasons, and quotations that explain or prove the main idea. Draw an umbrella: the main idea is the umbrella, and every major detail must fit under it. A statement covering only one or two details is too small (too narrow); one covering much more than the passage discusses is too big (too broad).

Talking point 4: Implied main ideas (3 minutes)

When no sentence states the point, learners list the details, ask “What do these have in common?” and “What does the author want me to understand?”, then write one sentence and test it with the umbrella.

Talking point 5: Summarizing (3 minutes)

A summary restates a text's main idea and key points in the reader's own words. Five steps: (1) state the main idea; (2) add two to four key points, roughly one per major section; (3) leave out examples, numbers, and quotations unless they are essential; (4) add no opinions or outside information; (5) check every statement against the text.

Talking point 6: The answer traps (4 minutes, during the examples)

Wrong answers on GED main idea and summary questions are usually too narrow (a true detail), too broad (bigger than the passage), not stated (outside knowledge or the reader's opinion), or distorted (a detail that has been changed or exaggerated). Name the trap aloud each time you eliminate a choice in the examples.

Worked examples

Example 1: Stated main idea in the first sentence

“Public libraries have quietly become some of the busiest job centers in many communities. On a typical weekday, visitors use library computers to search job listings and submit applications. Librarians help patrons format résumés and set up email accounts. Many libraries also host free workshops on interviewing and basic computer skills.”

Question: Which statement best expresses the main idea? (a) Librarians help people write résumés. (b) Public libraries now play a major role in helping people find work. (c) Libraries should receive more government funding. (d) Most people find jobs online.

Solution. Step 1, topic: public libraries. Step 2, what does the author say about them? They have become job centers (sentence 1). Step 3, umbrella test: computers for job searches, résumé help, and job workshops all fit under “major role in helping people find work.” Answer: (b). Choice (a) is too narrow (one detail). Choice (c) is not stated (an opinion the author never gives). Choice (d) is too broad and not stated.

Example 2: Main idea at the end, with a trap at the start

“Many people believe that getting in shape requires a gym membership or expensive equipment. A brisk 30-minute walk, however, raises the heart rate enough to strengthen the heart and lungs. Walking puts less stress on the knees than running, so people of most ages can do it. It requires nothing more than a pair of comfortable shoes. For many adults, walking may be the simplest way to build a regular exercise habit.”

Solution. Many learners will pick sentence 1, but it is a belief the author disagrees with, signaled by “however.” Sentences 2–4 give three reasons walking works: health benefit, low stress on joints, no cost. The last sentence pulls them together. Main idea: “For many adults, walking may be the simplest way to build a regular exercise habit.” Umbrella test: all three reasons fit under “simplest way.” Watch for transitions like however and but.

Example 3: Implied main idea, then a one-sentence summary

“In 2015, the town of Bellport had four grocery stores. Today it has one, on the far edge of town. Residents without cars now take two buses to reach it, a trip that can last more than an hour each way. Meanwhile, the number of convenience stores selling mostly packaged snacks has doubled. A recent survey found that fewer than half of Bellport families eat fresh vegetables on most days.”

Solution. No sentence states the point, so list the details (fewer stores, a long trip to the last one, more snack shops, fewer families eating vegetables) and ask what they share: healthy food has become hard to get. Implied main idea: “The loss of grocery stores has made it difficult for many Bellport residents to get fresh, healthy food.” Umbrella test: every detail fits. “Bellport has more convenience stores” is too narrow; “Americans do not eat enough vegetables” is too broad. One-sentence summary: “Since 2015, Bellport has lost three of its four grocery stores, and with only a distant store and more snack shops left, fewer families regularly eat fresh vegetables.”

Guided practice (15 minutes)

Read the passage aloud. Learners highlight each paragraph's main idea in one color and one key detail in another, then answer together.

[1] When people picture job training, many imagine a classroom. Apprenticeships take a different approach. An apprentice is hired by an employer and earns a paycheck while learning a skilled trade, such as electrical work, plumbing, or machining, from experienced workers on the job.

[2] For workers, the biggest advantage is that they do not have to choose between earning money and building skills. Most apprentices also take related classes, often paid for by the employer, and finish with a recognized credential. Because they have been working the whole time, they also finish with real experience to show future employers.

[3] Employers benefit as well. Training their own workers lets companies teach the exact skills they need. Many employers report that workers who complete apprenticeships stay with the company longer than workers hired in other ways, which saves the cost of constantly hiring and training new people.

  1. What is the topic? Answer: apprenticeships.
  2. What is the main idea of the whole passage? Answer: Apprenticeships combine paid work with skill training, and they benefit both workers and employers. (Paragraph 1 defines them; paragraphs 2 and 3 each give one group's benefits.)
  3. Which sentence states the main idea of paragraph 3? Answer: “Employers benefit as well.” Both later sentences describe a benefit to employers.
  4. Which detail supports the idea that apprenticeships help workers? Answer: any one of these: they earn a paycheck while learning; they finish with a recognized credential; they finish with real work experience.
  5. Write a two- or three-sentence summary. Sample: “Apprenticeships let people earn a paycheck while learning a skilled trade on the job. Workers gain skills, a credential, and experience without giving up income, and employers get workers trained in the exact skills they need who tend to stay longer.” Note that the trade examples are left out; they are not key points.

Independent practice (15 minutes)

Learners complete practice items 1–6. If a learner is stuck on item 1 or 6, ask, “Does that choice cover every paragraph, or just one?” If several learners click the first sentence on item 3, review it together: it is a transition, not the main idea.

Checks for understanding

  • Q: What is the difference between a topic and a main idea? Expected: A topic is a word or phrase naming the subject; a main idea is a complete sentence stating the author's point about that subject.
  • Q: An answer choice is true according to the passage but describes only one paragraph. Is it the main idea of the passage? Expected: No. It is too narrow; it fails the umbrella test.
  • Q: If no sentence states the main idea, what do you do? Expected: List the details, find what they share, write one sentence, test it.
  • Q: Name two things that do not belong in a summary. Expected: Any two of: your opinion; minor details such as specific examples, numbers, or quotations; information that is not in the text; copied sentences.
  • Q (thumbs up/down): “A good summary is about as long as the original.” Expected: Thumbs down. A summary is much shorter.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Choosing the first sentence automatically. Have the learner run the umbrella test on it, and point out hooks and opposing views that often open a paragraph (Example 2).

Choosing a true detail as the main idea. Ask, “Does this cover the other paragraphs too?” If not, it is too narrow.

Choosing an answer from background knowledge. Require learners to point to the line that says it. No line, no answer.

Adding opinions to summaries (“This is a great article,” “Cities should do this”). Give neutral sentence starters: “The author explains that …”, “According to the passage, …”.

Retelling everything or copying sentences. Set a limit of three to five sentences. Have learners cover the text, write from memory, then check for accuracy.

Differentiation

Support: Provide the frame “This text is mostly about ______, and the author's point is that ______.” Start with single paragraphs and read passages aloud. Have learners sort four ready-made statements as too narrow, too broad, not stated, or just right before writing their own.

Stretch: Have learners summarize the tree passage in exactly 25 words, state each paragraph's main idea and how it connects to the central idea, or write one wrong answer of each trap type and trade with a partner.

Teacher note: Use “main idea” for paragraphs and “central idea” for whole passages; the GED uses both.

How this shows up on the GED

About three-quarters of RLA reading passages are informational (articles, science and history writing, workplace documents, letters), and main idea questions appear with nearly all of them. Expect wording such as:

  • “Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?”
  • “Which detail from the passage best supports the idea that …?”
  • “Which sentence best states the main idea of paragraph 4?” (often a hot spot item)
  • “Which statement is the best summary of the passage?”
  • “How does paragraph 3 contribute to the development of the central idea?”
  • Drag-and-drop items that sort statements into “central idea,” “supporting detail,” and “not in the passage.”
  • Editing (drop-down) items that ask for the best topic sentence for a paragraph, or which sentence does not belong.

The extended response also depends on this skill: learners must summarize two arguments accurately before evaluating them.
student:
Why this skill matters

Almost every reading question on the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test comes back to one question: What is this text mostly about, and how do I know? If you can answer that, you will read faster, remember more, and spot wrong answers more easily. This week you will learn to find the main idea, identify the details that support it, and summarize a text in a few clear sentences.

Topic, main idea, and supporting details

TermWhat it isExample
TopicThe subject, in a word or phraseCity parks
Main ideaThe author's point about the topic, as a complete sentenceCity parks improve residents' health and bring neighbors together.
Supporting detailA fact, example, number, reason, or quotation that explains or proves the main ideaPeople who live near a park walk more each week than people who do not.

Quick check: A main idea can be true or false. A topic cannot. If what you wrote cannot be true or false, you have a topic, not a main idea.

On the GED, you will see main idea used for a paragraph and central idea used for a whole passage. They work the same way.

Where to find the main idea

  • The first sentence of a paragraph is the most common spot, but do not assume it.
  • After a hook or transition. Some paragraphs open with a story, a question, or a sentence like “That is only part of the story, however.” The main idea often comes right after.
  • The last sentence. Some authors give details first and then state the point.
  • Nowhere. Sometimes the main idea is implied, and you must put it into your own words.

For a whole passage, look at the title, the end of the first paragraph, and the last paragraph.

The umbrella test

Think of the main idea as an umbrella. Every important detail in the text must fit under it.

  • If a statement covers only one or two details, the umbrella is too small.
  • If a statement covers much more than the text talks about, the umbrella is too big.

When the main idea is implied

  1. List the main details in a few words each.
  2. Ask: “What do these details have in common?”
  3. Ask: “What does the author want me to understand?”
  4. Write one complete sentence.
  5. Test it with the umbrella.

How to write a summary

A summary restates the main idea and key points of a text in your own words. It is much shorter than the original.

  1. State the central idea in one sentence.
  2. Add two to four key points, usually one for each major part of the text.
  3. Leave out small examples, exact numbers, and quotations unless they are essential.
  4. Do not add your opinion or facts from outside the text.
  5. Check every sentence against the text. Is it accurate?

Strategy: Cover the text and write your summary from memory. Then uncover it and check. This keeps you from copying sentences and shows you what you really understood.

Watch out for these answer traps

TrapWhat it looks like
Too narrowA true detail from one paragraph, offered as the main idea
Too broadA big statement about the whole world, bigger than the passage
Not statedAn opinion or fact the passage never gives
DistortedA detail that has been changed, reversed, or exaggerated

Worked examples

Example 1: A stated main idea

“Your credit score can affect much more than whether you get a loan. Landlords often check credit before renting out an apartment. Some employers review credit reports when hiring for certain jobs. Insurance companies may use credit information when setting prices. Even utility companies may ask for a larger deposit from customers with low scores.”

Step 1. Topic: credit scores.

Step 2. What does the author say about them? Sentence 1: they affect much more than loans.

Step 3. Umbrella test: landlords, employers, insurance, and utilities are all “more than loans.” Every detail fits.

Main idea: A credit score affects many parts of life beyond borrowing money. A choice like “Landlords check credit before renting” is true, but it is too narrow.

Example 2: An implied main idea

“Ten years ago, Main Street in Corbin had six empty storefronts. Since then, more people have been able to work from home for employers in large cities, and several of them moved to Corbin for its lower rents. Today, Main Street has a coffee shop, a shared office space, and a bike repair store, and only one storefront is empty. The town's elementary school added two classrooms last fall.”

Step 1. List details: empty stores before; remote workers moved in; new businesses opened; school is growing.

Step 2. What do they share? The town is coming back to life since remote workers arrived.

Main idea: People who work from home have helped revive the small town of Corbin.

Check traps: “Corbin has a new coffee shop” is too narrow. “Working from home is better than working in an office” is not stated.

Example 3: Writing a summary

“[1] In many small towns, the fire department is made up mostly of volunteers who leave their jobs or homes when the alarm sounds. [2] Over the past twenty years, many of these departments have struggled to find enough volunteers. Required training now takes more hours than it once did, and more people work far from the towns where they live, so they cannot respond quickly. [3] To attract new members, some departments now offer small payments for each call, help with college costs, or free training that can lead to a paid career.”

Step 1, central idea: Volunteer fire departments are short of members and are trying new ways to recruit.

Step 2, key points: Paragraph 1: many small towns rely on volunteers. Paragraph 2: volunteers are harder to find because of longer training and long commutes. Paragraph 3: departments offer payments, college help, and training.

Summary: “Many small towns depend on volunteer firefighters, but these departments are struggling to find members because training takes longer and many people work far from home. To recruit, some departments now offer small payments, help with college, or free career training.”

A weak summary: “Firefighters are heroes, and everyone should volunteer.” This adds an opinion and leaves out the key points.

Try it

1. “Most people think of bees only as honey makers. Their bigger job, though, is pollination. As bees move from flower to flower, they carry pollen that many fruit and vegetable plants need to produce food. Without bees, farmers would harvest far fewer apples, almonds, and blueberries.” What is the topic, and which sentence states the main idea?

Show answer

Topic: bees. Main idea: “Their bigger job, though, is pollination.” The first sentence is a common belief that the author moves past (notice “though”). The last two sentences explain why pollination matters.

2. For the bee paragraph, label each statement too narrow, too broad, or just right. (a) Bees carry pollen. (b) Bees matter mostly because they pollinate the plants that produce much of our food. (c) Insects are important to the planet.

Show answer

(a) Too narrow: one detail. (b) Just right: covers every detail. (c) Too broad: the paragraph is about bees, not all insects.

3. “Last year, the clinic's phone line answered only about half of its calls. Patients waited an average of 40 minutes on hold. Many gave up and went to the emergency room instead, which cost them and the hospital far more.” State the implied main idea in one sentence.

Show answer

Sample: The clinic's overloaded phone line kept patients from getting care and sent them to the more expensive emergency room. Any answer that connects the phone problems to the costly emergency room visits is correct.

4. Which is the better summary of the fire department passage in Example 3, and why? (a) “Volunteer fire departments are having trouble finding members, so some are offering payments and training to attract them.” (b) “Required training now takes more hours than it once did.”

Show answer

(a). It states the central idea and the key response. Choice (b) is a single detail from paragraph 2, so it is too narrow to be a summary.
post:
Summary of key points

  • The topic is the subject in a word or phrase. The main idea (or central idea for a whole passage) is the author's point about the topic, stated as a complete sentence.
  • Main ideas are often in the first sentence, but they can follow a hook or transition, come at the end, or be implied.
  • Supporting details are the facts, examples, numbers, reasons, and quotations that explain or prove the main idea.
  • Use the umbrella test: the main idea must cover every important detail, and no more.
  • A summary gives the central idea and key points in your own words, with no opinions and no minor details.
  • Watch for the four traps: too narrow, too broad, not stated, and distorted.

Exit ticket

1. Is “school lunches” a topic or a main idea? Explain.

Show answer

A topic. It is a phrase, not a sentence, and it cannot be true or false.

2. Name two places in a paragraph where the main idea might appear besides the first sentence.

Show answer

Any two: right after a hook or transition, in the last sentence, or nowhere (implied).

3. An answer choice is a true fact from paragraph 2 of a six-paragraph passage. Why is it probably wrong for a central idea question?

Show answer

It is too narrow. It covers one paragraph, not the whole passage.

4. What is wrong with this summary sentence: “The author makes a great point that everyone should exercise”?

Show answer

It includes the reader's opinion (“great point”) and says nothing about the passage's actual key points.

5. List the steps for finding an implied main idea.

Show answer

List the details, find what they have in common, decide what the author wants you to understand, write one sentence, and test it with the umbrella.

Reflection

  • Which was harder for you this week: finding the main idea or writing a summary? What made it hard?
  • Think of a time you chose a wrong answer that “sounded true.” Which trap was it?
  • Where else in your life, at work, at home, or online, would summarizing help you?

This week's study plan

DayWhat to doTime
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. Redo the Try it problems without looking at the answers.25 min
Day 2Study the vocabulary. Read one news article and write its topic, main idea, and one supporting detail.25 min
Day 3Complete practice items 1–6. Read every explanation, even for items you got right.30 min
Day 4Complete practice items 7–12. For each miss, name the trap you fell into.30 min
Day 5Summary drill: choose two articles and write a three-sentence summary of each. Check them with the five summary steps.25 min
Day 6Take this week's Practice GED for Reasoning Through Language Arts under timed conditions.40 min, continue on Day 7 if needed
Day 7Finish the Practice GED if needed. Review every missed question and list the skills to work on.30 min

Test-taking strategy: Answer before you look

On a main idea or summary question, read the question, then state the answer to yourself in one sentence before you read the choices. Next, find the choice that matches your sentence. Finally, check that choice with the umbrella test. Wrong answers are written to sound reasonable. Having your own answer first keeps them from pulling you off track.

vocab.def: The subject of a text, usually named in a word or short phrase.
The most important point an author makes about the topic of a paragraph, stated as a complete sentence.
vocab.example: Public libraries now play a major role in helping people find work.

vocab.def: The main idea of a whole passage. The GED often uses this term.
vocab.example: Cities are starting to treat trees as necessary public equipment.

vocab.def: The sentence in a paragraph that states its main idea, often but not always the first sentence.
vocab.example: “Employers benefit as well.” opens a paragraph about how apprenticeships help companies.

vocab.def: A fact, example, number, reason, description, or quotation that explains or proves the main idea.
vocab.example: Homes shaded by trees used about 12 percent less electricity for cooling.

vocab.def: A main idea that the author writes directly in one sentence of the text.
vocab.example: “Your credit score can affect much more than whether you get a loan.”

vocab.def: A main idea the author does not state directly; the reader figures it out from the details.
vocab.example: Details about closed grocery stores and long bus trips imply that healthy food has become hard to get.

vocab.def: A short restatement of a text's central idea and key points in your own words, without opinions or minor details.
vocab.example: A three-sentence summary of a one-page article.

vocab.def: Restating one idea or sentence in your own words, at about the same length as the original.
vocab.example: “Trees catch rain” paraphrases “leaves and branches catch rainwater and slow its fall.”

vocab.def: Nonfiction writing that explains or gives facts, such as articles, reports, letters, and workplace documents.
vocab.example: A news article about city tree planting.

vocab.def: Closely connected to the main idea. A detail that is not relevant does not belong in the paragraph.
vocab.example: In a paragraph about a room's advantages, a sentence about repainting a different building is not relevant.

vocab.def: Based on the facts in the text, not on personal feelings or opinions. Summaries should be objective.
vocab.example: Objective: “The author explains that …” Not objective: “The author makes a great point.”

vocab.def: A word or phrase that connects ideas and signals a shift, such as however, also, or as a result.
vocab.example: “Cooling is only part of the story, however.”

notes:
Week 1 RLA Study Sheet: Main Idea, Details, Summarizing

Key terms

  • Topic: subject in a word or phrase
  • Main idea: author's point about the topic, as a sentence (can be true or false)
  • Central idea: main idea of a whole passage
  • Supporting detail: fact, example, number, reason, or quote that proves the main idea
  • Summary: central idea plus key points, in your own words, short and objective

Where main ideas live

  1. First sentence (most common)
  2. After a hook or transition
  3. Last sentence
  4. Implied (you write it)

For a passage: title, end of paragraph 1, conclusion.

Finding an implied main idea

  1. List the details.
  2. What do they have in common?
  3. What does the author want me to understand?
  4. Write one sentence.
  5. Umbrella test.

Writing a summary

  1. Central idea in one sentence
  2. Two to four key points
  3. Drop small examples, numbers, quotes
  4. No opinions, no outside facts
  5. Check accuracy against the text

Umbrella test: The main idea must cover every important detail. Too small = too narrow. Too big = too broad.

Answer traps

TrapSignAsk yourself
Too narrowTrue, but only one detail or paragraphDoes it cover the whole text?
Too broadAbout the whole world or a bigger subjectDoes the text really discuss all of this?
Not statedOpinion or outside knowledgeCan I point to where it says this?
DistortedA detail changed, reversed, or exaggeratedDoes it match the text word for word in meaning?

Strategy: Say the answer in your own words before reading the choices. Then match and test.

Common mistakes: picking the first sentence automatically; picking a true detail; using background knowledge; adding opinions to a summary.

stimuli.title: Shade Is Infrastructure: Why Cities Are Counting Their Trees
stimuli.html:
[1] On a July afternoon in Marlow Falls, a sidewalk in the Eastgate neighborhood measured 131 degrees Fahrenheit. Two miles away, on a tree-lined street in the Hillcrest neighborhood, the same kind of sidewalk measured 94 degrees. The air temperature in both places was almost the same. The difference was shade. Measurements like these are changing how city leaders think about trees. For decades, trees were treated as decoration, something to add after the “real” work of paving roads and laying pipes was done. Now a growing number of planners argue that trees are infrastructure: public equipment that a city needs in order to work, just like streetlights and storm drains.

[2] The most obvious service trees provide is cooling. A large tree can shade a roof, a wall, or a stretch of pavement for most of the day, and surfaces that stay out of direct sun absorb far less heat. When the walls and roof of a house stay cooler, the air conditioner inside does not have to run as long. In a study by the Marlow Falls electric utility, homes with mature trees shading their south and west sides used about 12 percent less electricity for cooling over one summer than similar homes without shade. Trees also release water vapor through their leaves, which cools the surrounding air by a few degrees, much as sweat cools skin.

[3] Cooling is only part of the story, however. Trees also help cities manage rain. During a storm, leaves and branches catch rainwater and slow its fall, and roots draw water down into the soil instead of letting it race across pavement. That matters because nearly every gallon that runs off a street ends up in the city's storm drains. When too much water arrives at once, the drains overflow and streets flood. Marlow Falls engineers estimate that the city's existing trees hold back enough runoff to delay a planned $40 million expansion of the drainage system by at least ten years.

[4] Shade also protects people. Heat kills more people in the United States than any other type of weather, and those most at risk are older adults, young children, outdoor workers, and anyone without reliable air conditioning. Cooler streets make it safer to walk to a bus stop, wait for a ride, or work outside. Doctors at Marlow Falls General Hospital reported that most emergency visits for heat illness during last summer's heat waves came from the city's three least-shaded neighborhoods. Researchers have also linked access to trees and green space with lower stress and more physical activity, although they note that many other factors affect health as well.

[5] The trouble is that these benefits are not shared equally. When Marlow Falls completed its first full tree count in 2023, it found that trees covered 41 percent of Hillcrest but only 9 percent of Eastgate. The pattern is common in American cities. Older, wealthier neighborhoods often have large trees planted generations ago, while neighborhoods built near highways, factories, or large parking lots have few. The residents with the least shade are frequently the ones who can least afford high cooling bills.

[6] To close that gap, Marlow Falls adopted a plan last year to plant 15,000 trees over the next ten years, with most of them going to neighborhoods where tree cover is below 20 percent. Planting is the easy part. Young trees need regular watering for their first three years, and many die without it. So the city is hiring and training local residents to care for new trees on their own blocks, which also creates jobs in the neighborhoods that need them most. A newly planted tree will not cast much shade for at least a decade. City forester Dana Whitfield says that is exactly why the work cannot wait. “Every year we put this off is a year of shade we never get back,” she said. “We are planting for the summers our kids will live through.”

(1) Starting Monday, March 3, our Tuesday and Thursday evening study hall will move from the library annex to Room 112 in the main building. The hours will stay the same, 6:00 to 8:30 p.m. In this memo, I want to explain the reasons for the move and what it will mean for you as a volunteer tutor.

(2) (A) Room 112 seats thirty people, compared with fifteen in the annex, so we will no longer have to turn learners away on busy nights. It also has twelve laptops that learners can use for online practice tests. The room is next to the east parking lot, which matters to learners who come straight from work and arrive just as study hall begins. The annex will be repainted next summer. Finally, the room has a whiteboard wall where tutors can work through problems with small groups.

(3) The move does come with one new responsibility. Because Room 112 is shared with a daytime English class, we must leave it exactly as we found it. Each volunteer (B) asked to arrive ten minutes early to set up the laptops and to return all materials to the supply cabinet before leaving. Please also make sure the laptops are plugged into the charging cart at the end of the evening so they are ready for the morning class.

(4) Learners will receive a printed notice about the new room during the last week of February, and signs in the annex will direct anyone who forgets. If a learner shows up at the annex during the first few weeks, please walk with that person to Room 112 so no one misses study time.

(5) Thank you for your flexibility. Many of our learners have told me that study hall is the most useful part of their week, and that is because of you. If you have questions about the move, please call me at extension 214 or stop by my office before March 3.

stimuli.title: Sleep on It: How Rest Helps the Brain Learn
stimuli.html:
[1] At 2 a.m., Luis is still at his kitchen table with a stack of flash cards. His GED Science test is in eight hours, and he has decided that every hour of sleep he skips is another hour of studying. Many test-takers make the same choice. A large body of research suggests, however, that Luis has the trade-off backward. Sleep is not time stolen from learning. It is one of the times when learning actually happens.

[2] For much of history, people assumed that sleep was simply the brain switching off, like a machine powered down for the night. That idea began to fall apart in the twentieth century, when scientists started recording the electrical activity of sleeping brains. The recordings showed that the brain stays busy all night. It moves through a repeating cycle of stages, including light sleep, deep sleep, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, completing one cycle about every 90 minutes. Each stage has its own pattern of activity, and researchers have spent decades working out what that activity accomplishes.

[3] One of its most important jobs is protecting new memories. When you learn something during the day, such as a new vocabulary word or the steps of a math problem, the memory is first held in a part of the brain called the hippocampus. This storage is temporary and fragile, a bit like a document that has been typed but not yet saved. During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay the day's new information and strengthen it, moving it into longer-term storage in the brain's outer layer, the cortex. Once a memory has been strengthened this way, it is much less likely to fade.

[4] Experiments support this idea. In one study, volunteers learned a list of forty word pairs, such as “ocean–lamp,” in the evening. Half of the group then slept for eight hours. The other half stayed awake for the same eight hours. When both groups were tested afterward, the people who had slept remembered about 20 percent more word pairs than those who had stayed awake. Researchers have repeated versions of this experiment many times with similar results: people who sleep after learning tend to remember more than people who do not.

[5] Different stages of sleep may help with different kinds of learning. Deep sleep, which is most common early in the night, appears especially important for facts and information, such as dates, definitions, and formulas. REM sleep, which grows longer in the early-morning hours, seems to help the brain connect ideas and practice skills, such as solving a new kind of problem. This is one reason a short night can be so costly. Someone who sleeps only four hours misses much of the REM sleep that normally comes in the final hours of a full night.

[6] For learners, the message is practical. Studying and then sleeping is a better plan than studying all night. A short review of key material in the evening, followed by a full night of rest, gives the brain a chance to do its overnight work. Spreading study over several days, with sleep in between, gives the brain several chances instead of one. Luis would likely remember more if he put down the flash cards, went to bed, and spent ten minutes reviewing them in the morning. Sleep is not a break from studying. It is part of studying.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Cities are starting to treat trees as essential infrastructure because trees provide measurable benefits, and some cities are working to spread those benefits more fairly.
Sidewalks in neighborhoods without trees can become dangerously hot during the summer.
Planting trees is a cheaper way to prevent flooding than expanding a city's storm drains.
Wealthy neighborhoods should pay to plant trees in neighborhoods that have fewer of them.
items.hint: Find the choice that fits over every paragraph, not just one. Paragraph 1 ends with the author's big claim.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the author's central claim. Paragraph 1 ends: planners “argue that trees are infrastructure: public equipment that a city needs in order to work.”

Step 2. Check the rest of the passage. Paragraphs 2–4 describe benefits (cooling, managing rain, protecting health). Paragraphs 5–6 explain that the benefits are unequal and describe Marlow Falls' plan to plant trees where cover is low.

Step 3. Umbrella test: only the first choice covers all six paragraphs. Correct.

The sidewalk choice is too narrow; it repeats one detail from paragraph 1. The flooding choice is distorted: paragraph 3 says trees may delay a drainage expansion, not that trees are a cheaper replacement, and it covers only one paragraph. The wealthy-neighborhoods choice is not stated; the passage never says who should pay.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 2, how do shade trees reduce the amount of electricity a home uses?
options: They keep the home's walls and roof cooler, so the air conditioner does not have to run as long.
They block cold winds, so the home's heater does not have to run as long.
They release water vapor that is collected and piped into the home to cool it.
They lower the price that the utility company charges for electricity.
items.hint: Reread the third sentence of paragraph 2.
items.explain:
Step 1. Go to paragraph 2. Sentence 2 says shaded surfaces “absorb far less heat.”

Step 2. Sentence 3 connects this to electricity: “When the walls and roof of a house stay cooler, the air conditioner inside does not have to run as long.” That matches the first choice. Correct.

The heater choice is not stated; the passage never mentions winter or wind. The water vapor choice is distorted: paragraph 2 says vapor cools “the surrounding air,” not that it is collected and piped indoors. The price choice is not stated; the homes used less electricity, but nothing says the price changed.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 3 that best states the main idea of that paragraph.
spans: Cooling is only part of the story, however.
Trees also help cities manage rain.
During a storm, leaves and branches catch rainwater and slow its fall, and roots draw water down into the soil instead of letting it race across pavement.
That matters because nearly every gallon that runs off a street ends up in the city's storm drains.
When too much water arrives at once, the drains overflow and streets flood.
Marlow Falls engineers estimate that the city's existing trees hold back enough runoff to delay a planned $40 million expansion of the drainage system by at least ten years.
items.hint: The first sentence links back to paragraph 2. Which sentence introduces the new point that the rest of the paragraph explains?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify what the paragraph is about. Every sentence after the first two is about rain: catching rainwater, runoff, overflowing drains, and the drainage expansion.

Step 2. Find the sentence that covers all of those details: “Trees also help cities manage rain.” Correct.

Step 3. Check the trap. “Cooling is only part of the story, however” is a transition. It connects to the cooling topic of paragraph 2 but does not say what this paragraph is about. The other sentences are supporting details; for example, the $40 million estimate is one piece of evidence, so it is too narrow.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the author states that the benefits of trees “are not shared equally.” Which detail from the passage best supports this statement?
options: “trees covered 41 percent of Hillcrest but only 9 percent of Eastgate”
“Young trees need regular watering for their first three years, and many die without it.”
“homes with mature trees shading their south and west sides used about 12 percent less electricity for cooling”
“leaves and branches catch rainwater and slow its fall”
items.hint: Look for a detail that compares two groups of people or places.
items.explain:
Step 1. Restate the claim: some places get more of the benefits of trees than others.

Step 2. Supporting this claim requires a comparison showing that one place has more trees than another. The detail “trees covered 41 percent of Hillcrest but only 9 percent of Eastgate” shows exactly that difference. Correct.

Step 3. The other details are true but support different points. The 12 percent electricity detail shows that trees save energy (paragraph 2), not that the savings are unequal. The rainwater detail explains how trees manage storms (paragraph 3). The watering detail explains why young trees need care (paragraph 6).

items.prompt: The author suggests that trees can save money for residents and for the city. Which two details support this idea? Select two answers.
options: Homes shaded by mature trees used about 12 percent less electricity for cooling over one summer.
The city's existing trees hold back enough runoff to delay a planned $40 million drainage expansion by at least ten years.
A sidewalk in Eastgate measured 131 degrees, while one in Hillcrest measured 94 degrees.
Trees covered 41 percent of Hillcrest but only 9 percent of Eastgate.
Young trees need regular watering for their first three years.
Marlow Falls plans to plant 15,000 trees over the next ten years.
items.hint: Look for details that mention lower bills or costs that are avoided or put off.
items.explain:
Step 1. Look for details about money: lower bills or avoided costs.

Step 2. Using 12 percent less electricity for cooling means lower electric bills for residents (paragraph 2). Correct. Delaying a $40 million drainage expansion by at least ten years puts off a large cost for the city (paragraph 3). Correct.

Step 3. The sidewalk temperatures show a difference in heat, not in money. The 41 percent and 9 percent figures show unequal tree cover. The watering and planting details describe the city's plan; they say nothing about savings.

items.prompt: Which choice is the best summary of the passage?
options: Planners increasingly see trees as necessary city infrastructure. Trees cool homes and streets, reduce energy use, absorb stormwater, and protect health. Because tree cover is uneven, Marlow Falls plans to plant 15,000 trees, mostly in low-shade neighborhoods, and is hiring residents to care for them.
Trees are the most important part of any city. Every city should follow the example of Marlow Falls and plant thousands of trees, because nothing else does as much to keep people healthy.
In Marlow Falls, a sidewalk in Eastgate reached 131 degrees while one in Hillcrest reached 94 degrees. Trees release water vapor through their leaves, which cools the air much as sweat cools skin.
Trees cool cities and absorb rain. Because Hillcrest has less tree cover than Eastgate, Marlow Falls plans to plant 15,000 trees in Hillcrest over the next ten years.
items.hint: A good summary is accurate, covers the whole passage, and contains no opinions.
items.explain:
Step 1. A summary must give the central idea, cover the key points of every major section, be accurate, and stay objective.

Step 2. The first choice states the central idea (trees as infrastructure), the benefits from paragraphs 2–4, the unequal coverage from paragraph 5, and the plan from paragraph 6. Every statement matches the text. Correct.

Step 3. The “most important part of any city” choice adds opinions (“every city should”) that the author never states. The sidewalk choice is too narrow; it lists two details from paragraphs 1 and 2. The last choice is distorted: paragraph 5 says Hillcrest has more tree cover (41 percent) than Eastgate (9 percent), and the plan targets low-cover neighborhoods, not Hillcrest.

items.prompt:
Read the draft memo. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): {{0}} Room 112 seats thirty people, compared with fifteen in the annex, so we will no longer have to turn learners away on busy nights.

Paragraph 3, blank (B): Each volunteer {{1}} asked to arrive ten minutes early to set up the laptops and to return all materials to the supply cabinet before leaving.

options: The new room offers several advantages over the annex.
The library annex was built more than forty years ago.
Many of our volunteers are retired teachers.
Please remember to sign in at the front desk each evening.
is
are
were
being

items.hint: For (A), read the rest of paragraph 2 and ask what all of its details describe. For (B), find the subject of the sentence and decide whether it is singular or plural.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: List what the rest of paragraph 2 describes: more seats, laptops, a location near parking, and a whiteboard wall. Step 2: Every one of these is a reason Room 112 is better than the annex. Step 3: The topic sentence must cover all of them: “The new room offers several advantages over the annex.” Correct. The other choices are off topic: the annex's age, the volunteers' backgrounds, and sign-in rules are not what paragraph 2 discusses.

Blank (B). Step 1: The subject is “Each volunteer.” Each refers to one person at a time, so the subject is singular. Step 2: The memo is written in the present tense (“we must leave it,” “Please also make sure”). Step 3: A singular, present-tense verb is needed: “Each volunteer is asked.” Correct. “Are” is plural. “Were” is plural and past tense. “Being” cannot serve as the main verb, so it would leave a sentence fragment.

items.prompt: Which sentence should be removed from paragraph 2 of the memo because it does not support the main idea of the paragraph?
options: Room 112 seats thirty people, compared with fifteen in the annex, so we will no longer have to turn learners away on busy nights.
It also has twelve laptops that learners can use for online practice tests.
The annex will be repainted next summer.
Finally, the room has a whiteboard wall where tutors can work through problems with small groups.
items.hint: Paragraph 2 is about why Room 112 is a better place for study hall. Which sentence is not about Room 112 at all?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the paragraph's main idea: Room 112 has advantages over the annex.

Step 2. Test each sentence. More seats: an advantage of Room 112. Laptops: an advantage. Location near the parking lot: an advantage. Whiteboard wall: an advantage.

Step 3. “The annex will be repainted next summer” is about the old space and a future project. It gives no reason Room 112 is better, so it is not relevant and should be removed. Correct. The whiteboard sentence begins with “Finally,” which signals the last item in the list of advantages, so it belongs.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Sleep is an active process that helps the brain strengthen and store new learning, so it is an important part of studying.
The sleeping brain moves through light sleep, deep sleep, and REM sleep about every 90 minutes.
Test-takers should never review any material in the evening before going to bed.
Scientists have not yet found any connection between sleep and memory.
items.hint: Look at how paragraph 1 and paragraph 6 end. Then check which choice fits every paragraph in between.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the stated claim. Paragraph 1 ends: “Sleep is not time stolen from learning. It is one of the times when learning actually happens.” Paragraph 6 ends: “Sleep is not a break from studying. It is part of studying.”

Step 2. Check the middle. Paragraph 2 shows the brain is busy during sleep; paragraph 3 explains how sleep strengthens memories; paragraph 4 gives experimental evidence; paragraph 5 explains how different stages help; paragraph 6 gives advice. The first choice covers all of this. Correct.

Step 3. The 90-minute choice is too narrow; it is one detail from paragraph 2. The “never review” choice is distorted: paragraph 6 actually recommends “a short review of key material in the evening.” The “no connection” choice contradicts paragraphs 3 and 4.

items.prompt: Drag each statement into the correct category based on the passage.
choices: Sleep plays an active role in helping the brain store what a person learns.
The brain completes one cycle of sleep stages about every 90 minutes.
In one study, people who slept after learning word pairs remembered about 20 percent more pairs than people who stayed awake.
Adults need at least ten hours of sleep the night before a test in order to pass it.
Drinking coffee while studying late at night improves memory.
items.hint: The central idea covers the whole passage. A supporting detail is a specific fact the passage gives. If you cannot point to it in the passage, it is not in the passage.
items.explain:
Central idea: “Sleep plays an active role in helping the brain store what a person learns.” This covers every paragraph and restates paragraph 1 (“one of the times when learning actually happens”).

Supporting details: The 90-minute cycle comes from paragraph 2 and supports the idea that the sleeping brain is busy. The word-pair study comes from paragraph 4 and supports the idea that sleep improves memory. Both are specific facts that develop the central idea.

Not in the passage: The passage never states how many hours of sleep a person needs to pass a test; “ten hours” does not appear anywhere. The passage never mentions coffee. These may sound reasonable, but neither can be found in the text.

items.prompt: A student is writing a summary of the passage. Which detail is least important to include in the summary?
options: Luis is studying flash cards at his kitchen table at 2 a.m.
During sleep, the brain strengthens new memories and moves them into longer-term storage.
People who sleep after learning tend to remember more than people who stay awake.
Studying and then getting a full night of sleep works better than studying all night.
items.hint: Which detail could you remove without losing any of the author's key points?
items.explain:
Step 1. A summary keeps the central idea and key points and leaves out minor details and examples.

Step 2. Test each choice. The memory-storage statement is the key point of paragraph 3. The “people who sleep remember more” statement is the conclusion of the research in paragraph 4. The “study, then sleep” statement is the main advice of paragraph 6. Removing any of these would leave out a key point.

Step 3. Luis at his kitchen table is an example used as a hook in paragraph 1 to draw readers in. The passage's point does not depend on Luis, so this detail is least important. Correct.

items.skill: How a paragraph develops the central idea
items.prompt: How does paragraph 4 contribute to the development of the central idea of the passage?
options: It provides experimental evidence that sleeping after learning improves memory.
It describes the different stages the brain moves through during a night of sleep.
It presents an opposing view that sleep has little effect on memory.
It gives practical advice for planning study time before a test.
items.hint: Paragraph 4 begins, “Experiments support this idea.” What idea, and what kind of support?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the first sentence of paragraph 4: “Experiments support this idea.” “This idea” refers back to paragraph 3: sleep strengthens new memories.

Step 2. The rest of paragraph 4 describes a study: people who slept after learning word pairs remembered about 20 percent more than people who stayed awake, and similar studies found similar results. This is experimental evidence supporting the central idea that sleep helps learning. Correct.

Step 3. The sleep-stages choice describes paragraphs 2 and 5, not paragraph 4. The opposing-view choice is wrong because paragraph 4 supports the link between sleep and memory. The practical-advice choice describes paragraph 6.
